item.text: {"case_id":"SPR00041","decision":"candidate","candidate_ranking":["C14","C13","C05"],"selected_candidate_label":"C14","confidence":0.97,"relationship_type":"both","rationale":"C14 plausibly supplied a concrete template for the child. Both veto memoranda concern private bills awarding a named claimant compensation for voluntarily supplying information or assistance that benefited federal governmental activity. They use closely parallel reasoning: valuable public-spirited assistance does not create an entitlement to compensation; the claimant is not materially distinguishable from numerous citizens who voluntarily furnish useful information; and approving an individual award would encourage inappropriate claims. The child expands this template by distinguishing a special monetary award from formal compensation and proposing acceptable revised legislation. C13 and C05 share private-claim and compensation machinery, but not the child's distinctive volunteer-information rationale.","shared_material":[{"child_excerpt":"The record demonstrates that the sum to be paid is not true compensation, but a monetary award for special services.","parent_excerpt":"The bill provides for payment ... for (1) compensation for services rendered by him ... in assisting and enabling the United States to prosecute successfully criminal proceedings","explanation":"Both frame a private relief payment as purported compensation for assistance rendered to the Government."},{"child_excerpt":"Each year there accrue to the Government the beneficial results of extraordinary services rendered by interested private citizens and organizations who volunteer much useful information and experience to the Congress, to its individual Members, and to the Executive Branch agencies as well.","parent_excerpt":"There is nothing to distinguish this case from any other case in which the Government receives from a private citizen information concerning wrongful action ... The vast majority of such proceedings are made possible by citizens who ... supply law enforcement officers with information","explanation":"This is a distinctive shared rationale: citizens commonly volunteer useful information that benefits governmental work, so one informant should not receive exceptional compensation."},{"child_excerpt":"I do not believe that claims for compensation for such volunteer services should be encouraged.","parent_excerpt":"Apart from the initial tip concerning the existence of a possible conspiracy ... it does not appear that claimant contributed anything to the successful prosecution and civil recovery.","explanation":"Both reject a compensation claim arising from voluntarily furnished information rather than a formal employment or contractual relationship."},{"child_excerpt":"While I cannot approve the bill in its present form ... I shall be glad to approve a bill which is by its terms an extraordinary monetary award for special service and which removes the tax-free status of the award.","parent_excerpt":"Even if claimant were to be treated as if he had commenced suit as an informer, he would be entitled to no more than the 10 percent of the civil recovery, whereas the bill proposes to award him 30 percent of that amount.","explanation":"Both conclude by indicating that some differently framed or limited recognition could be defensible while rejecting the compensation proposed by the enrolled bill."}]}
